"Hey Nineteen" was written by members Walter Becker and Donald Fagen, and released on their 1980 album Gaucho.

According to one reviewer's interpretation, the song "was about a middle-aged man's disappointment with a young lover ("Hey Nineteen, that's 'Retha Franklin / She don't remember the Queen of Soul / It's hard times befallen the Soul Survivors / She thinks I'm crazy but I'm just growing old")."

Steely Dan used a variety of musicians on their albums. On this track, Hugh McCracken played guitar, Rick Marotta was on drums, and Victor Feldman and Steve Gadd added percussion. Walter Becker also added guitar, and Donald Fagen played the Fender Rhodes electric piano and the synthesizer. Roger Nichols, who was one of the engineers on the Gaucho sessions, fashioned a drum machine they used on this track. Dubbed "Wendel," it was one of the first of its kind, and it allowed them to record Rick Marotta's drum parts and play them back with perfect precision.

Definitely not a baby bird.

First indication is that it is fully feathered, the fluff on its chest are full grown adult feathers, but they are puffed out in this picture, perhaps because the bird is a little cold and is trying to stay warm.

Second indication is edges of the beak. Baby birds have fleshy edges to the beak which are light colored, serving both the purpose of attracting the parent's bird attention due to the colour and effectively making the bird's mouth larger which makes it easier for the parent birds to put food in.

Third, it is standing correctly. Even young fledglings are not able to stand like an adult and often end up resting on their 'haunches'.

Fourth, even if this was a recently fledged bird, it would have tuffs of down atop its head leftover from when it was a chick. This down usually falls out anywhere from a week to a month after fledging, depending on the species.
